stories.episodeTitle: Treetop Treats / Eva the Ghost Catcher
stories.situation: Eva spots the one thing Ms. Featherbottom is missing, an art smock, and decides to win her the Golden Apron from the Treetop Treat Contest. Then the most talented artist in class, Sue Clawson, enters the same contest with a three-scoop masterpiece, and Eva's first attempt, everything-nachos, comes out a gloopy disaster.
stories.coping: Acorn carrot muffins rescue the round one, and the collision with Sue's ice cream ends the rivalry instead of the contest: both were entering for Ms. Featherbottom. Combined into one entry, muffins plus pecan butter ice cream plus sprinkles, they win, and the single Golden Apron goes exactly where Eva first pictured it, on her teacher.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: baking and contest romp plays 2-4; the competing-for-the-same-person reframe and the we-both-wanted-to-give-it beat land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis already centers the contest and the teacher gift; the script adds the Sue rivalry, the everything-nachos failure, and the collision-to-teamwork turn.
stories.synopsis: Eva enters the Treetop Treat Contest to win a Golden Apron for her teacher.
stories.perStorySynopsis: When Eva notices her teacher could use an art smock, she enters the Treetop Treat Contest to win the Golden Apron for her, then discovers her toughest competition is Sue Clawson, who is great at everything. Everything-nachos fail, acorn carrot muffins rise, and one collision later the two rivals realize they were baking for the very same teacher. One combined treat and one shared victory later, the Golden Apron lands where it belongs, and Eva's diary gets the best kind of ending, the kind you bake together.

stories.episodeTitle: Treetop Treats / Eva the Ghost Catcher
stories.situation: A white blur keeps flashing through Treetopington's best spots, the fun nest, the birdbath, the snack stand, and Eva is certain it is a ghost. Jacob keeps saying he does not think it is one, and Eva is so sure she is right that she does not stop to listen.
stories.coping: The ghost map turns out to be a friend map: the blur follows the welcome map Eva's mom made, and it is Kiera, the new neighbor, exploring town at full speed. Eva apologizes to Jacob for not listening, announces town-wide that there is no ghost, and opens the flaptastic fun nest with the fastest new friend in Treetopington.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: ghost-hunt chase comedy plays 2-4; the confident-mistake arc, not listening to the friend who was right, and the new-neighbor payoff land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis names the hunt; the script supplies the map clue, the Jacob-was-right admission, and the public no-ghost announcement.
stories.synopsis: Eva and her friends hunt a ghost that is haunting their fun nest.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Something fast, white, and undeniably spooky is flashing all over Treetopington, and the flaptastic fun nest cannot open with a ghost on the loose. Eva becomes a ghost catcher, Jacob becomes the friend nobody listens to, and the chase barrels through birdbaths, snack stands, and the world's largest pine cone. The trail, it turns out, is a welcome map, and the ghost is Kiera, the new neighbor, seeing the town Eva loves at a speed worth apologizing for. The fun nest opens, the flag goes up, and the town gains both an answer and a friend.

stories.situation: Eva hears her parents call Humphrey a great helper and wants the same warm blanket around her heart, so she appoints herself co-babysitter for Baby Mo's big night. Her super helpful list, flapping jacks, rocking nests, lullabies, even pretending to be asleep, only makes the wide-awake baby more awake, and the sun is coming up with her promise broken.
stories.coping: Out of list, Eva has to watch Humphrey's quiet answer work: Baby Mo just needed to be held by his big brother. At sunrise she gives the credit away honestly, telling their parents it was all Humphrey, then declares her list super unhelpful in her diary without a hint of bitterness. The dream team gets its feather ruffle shuffle after all.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: wide-awake-baby comedy plays 2-4; the helper-credit arc, doing less to earn more, and Eva's genuine praise for Humphrey land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'tries to help' is the frame; the script supplies the escalating list, the list running out, and Eva handing Humphrey the credit she wanted for herself.
stories.synopsis: Eva tries to help put Baby Mo to bed.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Eva wants what Humphrey has, the words great helper, so she joins his babysitting shift armed with a numbered list of sleep tricks. Every trick makes Baby Mo more awake: flapping jacks, rocking nests, a lullaby with guitar, even owlets pretending to sleep, which only invites a baby to wake them. As the sun rises on a broken promise, the answer turns out to be the one thing that was never on the list, and Eva finds that saying her brother figured it out feels warmer than she expected.

stories.situation: Eva and Lucy are picked as flower owlets and go all in on razzle-dazzle: armloads of petals, feather crowns, a wow walk choreographed by Baby Mo himself. Then the wind takes every single petal right as the guests arrive, and being flower owlets with no flowers is just being owlets.
stories.coping: Looking at the bride and groom resets the whole plan: they are the stars, not us. The crowns they made for themselves go on Ms. Featherbottom and Mr. Swoopington instead, the walk is a plain skip-flap-scatter with the last few petals, and the diary lands it: tonight was not about the razzle-dazzle, it was about being part of their night.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: petal-scattering and wow-walk comedy plays 2-4; the spotlight-reframe and the give-the-crown-away turn land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a special role' hides the showmanship escalation, the wind disaster, and the bride-and-groom-first resolution. vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
stories.synopsis: Ms. Featherbottom invites Eva and Lucy to play a special role in her wedding.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Being asked to be flower owlets at Ms. Featherbottom's wedding calls for maximum razzle-dazzle, and Eva and Lucy deliver: bundles of petals, self-made crowns, and a wow walk borrowed from a baby brother's waddle. Then the wind empties their baskets in front of the arriving guests. The recovery is not a replacement plan but a perspective shift, because the wedding was never their show. The crowns go where the wow belongs, on the bride and groom, and two owlets discover that scattering the last few petals for someone you love is the whole job.

stories.situation: Eva is honored to carry the class acorn, just like the littlest owlet in the founding story of Treetopington, and decides one acorn is not enough: she will secretly plant a whole forest. But acorns are hard to plant alone, and the surprise is discovered mid-dig, ruined before it is revealed.
stories.coping: Ms. Featherbottom releases the surprise gracefully: it does not matter whether it is a surprise. The whole class joins the forest planting, Eva's diary reframes the day, she thought she should do it alone like the littlest owlet, but it is more special to do it together, and someday owls from far and wide will rest on what they planted.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: digging and acorn comedy plays 2-4; the secret-project-backfire, being seen before ready, and the alone-versus-together lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'plan a secret project' names the setup; the script adds the acorn-carrier honor, the forest upgrade, and the caught-mid-dig turn that reframes the surprise. retagged: 'excited, embarrassed' to 'happy, embarrassed' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed). vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
stories.synopsis: A story time character inspires Eva to plan a secret project.
stories.perStorySynopsis: When the class learns their big oak tree grew from one little owlet's planted acorn, Eva gets the honor of planting the next one. She quietly decides to top the story: a whole secret forest, planted solo, revealed to gasps. Digging alone is harder than stories let on, and getting caught kneeling in the dirt deflates the big reveal entirely. What she gets instead is better than gasps, an entire class grabbing acorns, and a first lesson in the difference between a surprise and a gift you build together.

stories.situation: Eva invents the Treetop Swap so nobody has to throw away what someone else needs, and Humphrey keeps offering his organizing system. Every offer lands the same way: it is her idea, and she wants to do it her way, right up until the swap pile becomes a messy mountain and she cannot remember who wanted the owlball.
stories.coping: Humphrey wins her over the moment she asks, and his reassurance does the identity repair: it is still your idea no matter how you do it. Rows for seeing, lists for haves and wants, purple boots on the want-it list, and the swap turns into the ginormous success Eva wanted, finished with a puzzle they solve together, edges first.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: swap-chaos comedy plays 2-4; the my-idea pride, the overwhelmed turn, and the help-does-not-take-ownership lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Humphrey's talent comes in handy' is the outcome; the script's spine is Eva refusing help three times, the mountain of stuff, and the it-is-still-your-idea reassurance. vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
stories.synopsis: Humphrey's talent comes in handy during a Treetopington event.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Eva's new event, the Treetop Swap, runs on one rule: old to you, new to someone else. It also runs directly into Humphrey's offers of a system, which Eva declines with growing firmness, because the swap is her idea and her way is working exactly how she wants it. The pile disagrees. Buried in a mountain nobody can see into, with requests slipping through her memory, Eva asks for the system herself and hears the sentence every kid with a big idea needs: it is still your idea, no matter how you do it.

stories.situation: Kiera's first pet, a hedgehog named Jelly, makes Eva a teacher: Pet School opens with lessons on feeding, playing, and tricks. But Baxter discovers wing snacks on his own, Jelly and Kiera invent their own games, and the pets keep choosing Kiera's way, until Eva quietly decides the student has outgrown the teacher and nearly goes home.
stories.coping: Baxter follows Eva away from the fun and answers the wobble without a word: he still chooses his person. Kiera hands the identity back too, best teacher ever, because Eva taught her the part that matters most, loving your pet. They graduate to lesson four and to a school where both of them teach.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: pet-school comedy plays 2-4; the outgrown-teacher wobble, the should-I-just-go-home beat, and the both-of-us-teach resolution land 5-7. vocabulary gap: the beat is closest to jealousy or feeling inadequate, neither on the approved 16-term list, so tagged disappointed/proud as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: 'leans on Eva for caretaking advice' omits the student-surpasses-teacher turn and Eva's near-exit. vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).

stories.perStorySynopsis: A new hedgehog named Jelly turns Eva into the founder of Pet School, with a curriculum built from life with Baxter. The answer arrives on quiet wings, a best friend who followed her out of the fun, and a student who says the loving-pet part was always hers to give. Pet School ends the night with two teachers.

stories.situation: Dad carves a picture frame, and Eva wants to fill it with a photo as good as Mom's famous flower shot. The garden's moonflower is the perfect subject, but it opens only in moonlight, for a few moments, and when the moment finally comes, the picture is missed by a beak.
stories.coping: Mom does not fix it, she just keeps the camera out, and the night fills up with practice shots, silly faces, a pine-cone race, and memories saved to the diary. Looking back at them changes the ask: Dad's frame gets a photo of his favorite photographers having fun, and Eva decides memories beat a million-zillion flower photos.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: blurry-practice and silly-face comedy plays 2-4; the missed-once-chance disappointment and the memories-are-the-picture lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'a photography journey' undersells the moonflower's only-opens-in-moonlight stakes, the exact missed moment, and the frame-filling resolution.
stories.synopsis: Eva and her mom embark on a photography journey.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Dad's handmade frame needs one flaptastic photo, and Eva knows which one: a flower like Mom's, ideally the garden's legendary moonflower, which opens for a few moonlit moments only. A mother-daughter adventure of practice shots, cloud-watching, and statue-still waiting follows, and the flower opens exactly on schedule, for everyone but the camera. The ride home is quiet until the diary comes out, and the pictures they forgot they were taking turn out to be the ones Dad wants framed.

stories.episodeTitle: Nest Buddies / Game Night Under the Stars
stories.situation: Eva draws Sue as her nest buddy for her first night away from home and sees her opening: be the best nest buddy ever. But Sue is so Sue about it, already-built nest, snacks for the whole troop, honey-glazed pecans, and Eva's one sticky pine cone cannot compete, sap-stuck wings and all.
stories.coping: The one-upping stops when the truth does: Eva says it plainly, you are the best nest buddy ever, and Sue's answer dismantles the contest, she made her twig chairs from the twigs Eva carried and was just about to eat that pine cone. Neither one has to be the best, and with the worry gone Eva finally enjoys the trip and the sunrise.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: nest-building and sap-stuck comedy plays 2-4; the comparison spiral (I will never be a better nest buddy than Sue) and the compete-versus-enjoy reframe land 5-7. vocabulary gap: the felt emotion is closest to envy or feeling not-good-enough, neither on the approved 16-term list, so tagged disappointed/frustrated as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: 'works hard to impress Sue' is the engine; the script adds the repeated being-outdone beats and the mutual-credit turn. vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
stories.synopsis: On a Hoot Troop trip, Eva works hard to impress Sue.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Eva's first overnight trip comes with a Hoot Troop tradition, a nest buddy to take care of, and Eva plans to be the best one in troop history. Her nest buddy is Sue, who is best at everything, navigation, sunscreen, snack spectaculars, and every Eva effort lands one step behind. A sap-glued pine cone and two stuck wings slow the race down just enough for the truth to come out, and it turns out Sue has been using Eva's twigs, eating Eva's pine cone, and feeling out-nest-buddied herself. Nobody has to be the best, and the sunrise is better that way.

stories.episodeTitle: Nest Buddies / Game Night Under the Stars
stories.situation: Game night has owlball at the end of it, and Eva hurries through every game before it like the pace is the point. Slow, careful Jacob stretches, waits, retrieves a special new owlball, then flaps it into a sap-covered branch, and Eva's rush-to-fix ideas, pulling, kicking, make it worse.
stories.coping: The turnaround is Eva handing the clock back: take as much time as you need to think. Jacob's answer uses the sap itself, a vine stuck to the ball, tugged like tug-the-vine, and it works. Her diary lands the lesson in her own voice: Jacob does not move at my speed, and that is a good thing. The night ends with a brand-new game, vineball.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: game-night romp plays 2-4; the hurrying-versus-thinking arcs and the protect-his-time-to-think beat land 5-7. retagged under the ratified 18-term vocabulary (impatience added 2026-11-11); impatience was previously flagged as an off-list gap. script_vs_synopsis: 'team up to solve a sudden problem' hides that the rush itself caused the problem and that slowing down was the fix. retagged: 'impatient, excited' to 'impatient, happy' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
stories.synopsis: The owlets compete in a series of games and team up to solve a sudden problem.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Game night under the stars ends with owlball, the best game there is, so Eva sprints through tug-the-vine and acorn roll to get there faster. The pace falls apart around Jacob, who stretches, double-checks for sap, and finally gets his new special owlball stuck exactly where he feared. Every quick fix wedges it deeper, and the game only resumes when Eva gives the slowest owlet in Treetopington the one thing she never gives anyone, time. His sap-and-vine rescue works, the diary gets a new entry about good things that take a while, and vineball is born.

stories.episodeTitle: Eva's Big Catch / Carlos's Juice Stand
stories.situation: Eva is finally old enough for the mushroom-catching trip with Grandma, training pole and all, and arrives carrying the photo of Humphrey's famous Big One from last year. Humphrey catches another big one while Eva's pole snags, her heavy prize turns out to be a rock, and her only catch is the smallest mushroom anyone has ever seen. The diary wobble is bare: Humphrey will always be Grandma's favorite.
stories.coping: Grandma melts the comparison whole: it does not matter if you catch big mushrooms, small mushrooms, or none at all, and no, there is no favorite grandowlet, she loves them both this much (wings wide). The tiny mushroom becomes a necklace she will always wear to remember this special time with her grandowlet Eva, and the photo says teeny tiny mushroom.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: rock-catch and chant comedy plays 2-4; the favorite-grandchild worry and the no-favorites, wings-wide reassurance land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'mushroom-catching mission' is the frame; the script adds the training pole, the Big One photo, the rock catch, and the necklace resolution. vibe provisional: drafted as warm, mapped to the guide's calm/silly/energetic vocabulary (vibe rule undecided).
stories.synopsis: Grandma leads Humphrey and Eva on a mushroom-catching mission.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Eva's first mushroom-catching trip with Grandma comes with a training pole, a famous sibling trophy to live down, and a heart full of one question: is Humphrey the favorite? While Humphrey lands another Big One, Eva snags a branch, catches a rock, and finally nets a mushroom so small it needs a second look. Then Grandma says the thing that fixes the whole day, there is no favorite, the love comes in equal amounts, and the smallest mushroom in the forest becomes a necklace built for exactly one grandowlet.

stories.episodeTitle: Eva's Big Catch / Carlos's Juice Stand
stories.situation: Carlos needs someone to run his beloved juice stand for one night, and Eva volunteers with an upgrade in mind: more kinds of juice than his one blueberry. To fit them all in, she skips his steps one by one, the tasting, the full press, the pine sap, until the stand is serving cran-pepper-anchovy delight and the customers are gone.
stories.coping: Carlos comes back from his grandma's and diagnoses it kindly: all the steps are important, and they took him a long time, and a lot of blech, to figure out. One new juice, made together with every step kept, becomes Happy Sappy Peachberry Juice, the customers return, and Eva's diary credits the whole thing to doing all of the steps.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: wild-flavor comedy plays 2-4; the shortcut-costs-customers arc and the steps-were-earned lesson land 5-7. emotion drawn from the ratified 18-term list (impatience added 2026-11-11). script_vs_synopsis: 'shakes things up' names the experiment; the script supplies the step-skipping cascade, the empty-stand low, and Carlos's blech backstory.
stories.synopsis: Eva shakes things up at the local juice stand.
stories.perStorySynopsis: One night behind Carlos's juice stand is not enough time for Eva to serve his way, so she speeds up: more flavors, fewer steps, no tasting, a little less pressing, who needs the pine sap anyway. The customers get surprises like cherry-pepper and blueberry onion, and they vote with their wings. Carlos returns from his grandmother's to an empty stand and a confession, and instead of scolding, he shares how long his steps took to earn, then invites one new juice, made properly, together. Happy Sappy Peachberry Juice brings everybody back.

stories.situation: Eva's first sleepover runs on a list of super-duper plans, and the plans fail in order: no clouds for cloud-watching, paper too wet to paint, and Baby Mo finds the treasure-hunt pine cone before the hunt begins. While Eva scrambles to the next idea, her guests are playing, and she almost misses a whole sleepover of fun happening without her.
stories.coping: The reveal arrives in the guests' own voices: daytime leaf-jumping is super-duper, and this is the most fun sleepover ever. Eva's diary does the honest math, it did not matter that her plans were not super or duper, because her friends know how to have fun and do not need her to make it for them. She joins the game she was busy managing, and the late-arriving clouds get written into a cloudy story.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: plan-flop comedy plays 2-4; the hosting anxiety, the missed-fun reveal, and the friends-are-already-fun lesson land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'hosts her first sleepover' hides the plan-by-plan collapse, the literal it's-hopeless low, and the fun-was-happening-without-me turn.
stories.synopsis: Eva hosts her first sleepover.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Eva has planned her first sleepover down to the leaf piles, and the universe declines to cooperate: cloudless skies, wet watercolors, and a baby brother who wins the treasure hunt solo. The rescue is not a plan at all, it is the discovery that the sleepover has been fun the entire time, and the hostess finally jumps into the leaf pile she was too busy to notice.

stories.situation: Lantern day at school should be Lucy's showcase, but her blackberry-paint idea sends Eva recruiting her for Carlos, Sue, Jacob, and Kiera, one classmate at a time, without ever asking Lucy first. Eva's own sky lantern stays blank until Lucy, out of time for her Springtime Wonder-lantern, finally says she cannot help right now, and Eva cannot understand why.
stories.coping: Lucy explains it plainly: she spent all her time on everyone else's lanterns and now has none for her own. Eva owns the pattern, I should have asked you before I said yes for you, hands over her own petals, and solves her stars herself with a twig and a what-would-Lucy-do. Lucy gets the switch, the thanks, and the choice next time, because helping is hers to give.

stories.situation: One seed-catching save puts Eva on the front page of the Treetopington Times, and one headline stops feeling like enough. She chases the next story, owlball over the world's largest pine cone, acorn stacking, both crash, and then she hands the paper a better story, Sue and Carlos's brand-new pumpkin seed bread, and feels the small honest ache: I wish the story was about me.
stories.coping: Watching her shared story work, the whole town baking the recipe, teaches the reframe: what goes in the paper are stories that make owls' lives better, not stories about being seen. The ache gets said out loud to Mom, and it gets outgrown in the same scene as Eva recommends Lucy's dance for the next front page.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (felt-energy draft; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: acorn-stacking and headline comedy plays 2-4; the enough-vs-more arc, the named envy, and the share-the-story turn land 5-7. vocabulary gap: the confession is closest to envy, not on the 18-term list, so tagged disappointed/excited as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: 'winds up on the front page' undersells the second-fame chase, the two failed stunts, and the generosity resolution. retagged: 'disappointed, excited' to 'disappointed, proud' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).

stories.coping: Toad's confession, I have ruined everything, gets met exactly right: Frog names the kindness behind the accident, you wanted to do something nice for us, and solves the melting with a walk instead of a wait. They eat the ice cream at the stand the moment it is scooped, two chocolate cones, no melting, no waiting, and both are glad the scary thing was Toad.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: melting-cone monster comedy plays 2-4; the ruined-gift guilt and the kindness-behind-the-accident line land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'melty disaster' is the midpoint; the script adds the one-of-every-flavor decision, the monster-on-the-path panic, and the eat-it-at-the-stand fix.
stories.synopsis: Toad's delivery of refreshing ice cream to Frog turns into a melty disaster.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Choosing one flavor is impossible for Toad, so he chooses all of them, a towering gift for Frog on a blazing hot day. The walk home goes badly one drip at a time until a cone-covered Toad becomes the monster of the meadow, pursued by everyone he likes. When the truth and the puddle are revealed, Frog does what best friends do, spots the kindness inside the accident, and finds the one fix that beats the sun: ice cream eaten exactly where it is scooped.

stories.situation: Toad's favorite jacket loses a button on a walk, and only the exact button will do: the search retraces the whole day, through the sneezy meadow, the dark woods, and the river, turning up buttons that are black, two-holed, small, and square, everything except his. Toad declares they will never find it while Frog refuses to quit.
stories.coping: The answer is anticlimactic and true: the button has been on Toad's floor the whole time. He does the repair properly, returning the found buttons, sewing on his own, then handing Frog the jacket itself with every button sewn extra tight, because you are my favorite friend. The day ends with two friends choosing a walk, buttons intact.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: wrong-button comedy plays 2-4; the search-fatigue low and the give-the-jacket apology land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'great lengths' is the engine; the script adds the four wrong-button tests, the whole-world-covered-with-buttons low, and the jacket gift.
stories.synopsis: Frog and Toad go to great lengths to find a lost button.
stories.perStorySynopsis: A missing button on a favorite jacket sends Frog and Toad back over every step of their day, and every finding is wrong: too black, too few holes, too small, too square. The world, Toad concludes, is covered in buttons, none of them his, and the search ends the way hard days do, at home, where the button has been on the floor all along. What Toad does with the relief is the story: a jacket handed over with its buttons sewn on extra tight, for the friend who never stopped looking.

stories.situation: The most beautiful first day of spring ever is passing while Toad sleeps straight through it, and Frog is lonely without him. Toad counters every invitation with half past spring, a time that does not exist, and Frog has already proven he is excellent at waiting.
stories.coping: Waiting alone loses to a small forgivable fraud: Frog tears the calendar pages so it reads half past spring, and Toad, convinced, gets up and out. On the walk he works out the truth, it is not really half past spring, and forgives it instantly, it is still very beautiful, and I am glad you got me out of bed.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: bed-pushing and calendar comedy plays 2-4; the loneliness of missing a friend, the trick, and Toad's graceful catch of it land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'Frog wants Toad to spend the first day of spring with him' hides the wait-all-day structure, the calendar fraud, and Toad's seeing-through-it ending. retagged: 'lonely, hopeful' to 'lonely, frustrated' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
stories.synopsis: Frog wants Toad to spend the first day of spring with him.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Spring arrives in full glory, and Toad greets it from under a blanket, negotiating for half past spring, a time that is not on any clock. Frog waits beautifully, then waits badly, tearing calendar pages to make the impossible time arrive. Out on the meadow, Toad notices the cold, then the calendar, then the truth, and lets him off entirely: it is still very beautiful, and being woken into spring with a friend was worth the trick.

stories.situation: A story about brave Sir Toad and brave Squire Frog raises the question, are we brave? and the test is the tippy top of Mount Gloom, climbed without an umbrella, on a day of dark caves, glowing yellowish eyes, and rocks that tumble bigger and bigger.
stories.coping: Each scare gets answered the way the book heroes would, together: we are not afraid, mostly truthfully, with the cave and its lonely monster behind them. At the top, brave is confirmed, and the punchline is asking to be brave back at Toad's house, where two friends shelter from the storm they climbed into, feeling very brave together.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: cave-and-rock comedy plays 2-4; the are-we-brave question, pretending-not-afraid, and the sheltering-together ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'to prove they're brave' is the setup; the script adds the story-within-story, the cave monster, and the run-for-dessert retreat.
stories.synopsis: To prove they're brave, Frog and Toad set off to climb Mount Gloom.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog and Toad read about brave Sir Toad and brave Squire Frog and wonder the obvious: are we brave? The test writes itself, the tippy top of Mount Gloom, no umbrella, in the rain. There are dark caves (one occupied by a monster who mostly wanted company), rocks that tumble bigger and bigger, and wind that is too windy, and the two keep answering it the story way, together, we are not afraid. The summit certifies their bravery just in time for them to run back down and be brave indoors, where the cocoa is.

stories.situation: Toad plants his very first seeds and meets the gap between quite soon and now: nothing grows. He shouts instructions underground, decides the seeds are afraid, of the dark, then of the rain, and works through the whole comfort catalogue, firefly night lights, stories in the rain, poetry, silly faces, and a full hootenanny.
stories.coping: Morning brings green: the sprouts are up. Frog floats the gentle correction, maybe they were not afraid, maybe they just needed time to grow, and Toad reframes his waiting as work: he kept them company, read them stories, played them music. A gardener is born, and he is off to find a tuba for the garden.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shouting-at-seeds comedy plays 2-4; the waiting-versus-doing lesson and the reframed hard work land 5-7. emotion drawn from the ratified 18-term list (impatience added 2026-11-11). script_vs_synopsis: 'thinks the seeds are afraid' is Toad's theory; the script supplies the quite-soon confusion, the full care-ritual catalogue, and the time-to-grow reveal.
stories.synopsis: Toad thinks the seeds in his new garden are afraid to grow.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Toad plants his first garden with total confidence and zero patience, and the seeds respond to neither. Clearly they are afraid: of the dark (firefly disco), of the rain (bedtime stories), of silence (poems, songs, silly faces). When the sprouts finally arrive, so does the quieter truth, the seeds were not scared, they were growing at seed speed. Toad hears it, keeps his version too, and marches off to buy a tuba, because a garden this well cared for deserves music.

stories.situation: Rabbit's cake smells wonderful but is for a very special day, Tuesday, and waiting a whole day is impossible. Frog invents Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day and bakes with total confidence and no skill: eggs with shells, milk floods, sugar chaos, while Toad watches, wincing, and finally says the hard thing.
stories.coping: The confession, I do not know how to bake a cake, is met with joy instead of mockery: Toad takes over and does it together, until Frog names the takeover, it cannot be Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day when Toad bakes the cake. Toad makes it right with his own strange, hard, not-very-sweet cake, and Frog calls it the best he has ever had, a cake he will always remember.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shell-egg and lumpy-batter comedy plays 2-4; the kind-failure confession, the taken-over feeling named out loud, and the remembered-cake ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'even though he doesn't know how' is the setup; the script adds the Tuesday obsession, the full baking disaster, and the mutual cake preference swap. retagged: 'embarrassed, kind' to 'embarrassed, frustrated' per the ratified 18-term vocabulary (off-list terms removed).
stories.synopsis: Frog wants to bake a cake for Toad, even though he doesn't know how.
stories.perStorySynopsis: One whiff of Rabbit's Tuesday cake sends Frog to the kitchen on a mission of love, Frog Bakes a Cake for Toad Day, though his recipe knowledge ends at the word flour. Shells in the bowl, milk over the rim, sugar everywhere, and a guest of honor trying very hard to be polite. The day gets rescued by honesty in both directions: Frog admits he cannot bake, Toad admits being taken over does not feel like together, and the lumpy cake they share ends up the best either has ever had.

stories.situation: A homemade kite, a field of robin critics, and a wind that has to be summoned by licking a finger: the first flights crash, and Toad absorbs the verdict that the kite lacks aerodynamics and might as well be thrown away. Frog keeps prescribing confidence, plus running, waving, and shouting up, kite, up.
stories.coping: The very, very last try works, and the kite's reward is dragging both friends into the sky. The rescue chain grows one neighbor at a time until Frog declares the real decision: the kite goes on its adventure without them, everyone lets go on the count of three, and the pair land on the honest summary, flying it took work, confidence, and running and shouting and jumping, and it was fun. Only a little bit of fun.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: kite-crash and dog-walked-by-kite comedy plays 2-4; the doubters-versus-confidence arc and the letting-go ending land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'despite some doubting Robins' names the hecklers; the script adds the summon-the-wind bit, the whole-town rescue chain, and the deliberate let-go.
stories.synopsis: Frog and Toad attempt to fly their homemade kite despite some doubting Robins.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog has confidence in the homemade kite, Toad has a face full of meadow, and the robins have notes: too heavy, too many holes, no aerodynamics. After every crash there is one more very, very last try, and the try that works lifts them both clean off the ground. The kite, it turns out, also has confidence, and a whole neighborhood grabs the string before Frog and Toad choose the ending they want, letting go, so the kite can reach the top of the sky on its own.

stories.situation: A walk on the wrong path leaves Frog and Toad lost in the woods. Toad cycles through what to do, what to do, and misses lunch in the forecast, while Gopher asks the perfect unhelpful question: do you not know where you are, or not know where you are going?
stories.coping: Frog does not pretend the feeling away, he re-names the day: explorers. The unusual way turns out to be blueberries tested for safety, a babbling brook, a nap in the grass, and maple seeds spinning, and by dusk Toad thanks him for a pleasant afternoon. The exit line carries the whole lesson: you are never truly lost when you are with a friend.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: lost-in-the-woods comedy plays 2-4; the staying-calm attempt, the explorer reframe, and the friend-is-the-answer line land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'handles being lost differently' is the contrast; the script adds the two-kinds-of-lost Gopher gag, the explorer conversion, and the never-truly-lost close.
stories.synopsis: Frog handles being lost differently than Toad.
stories.perStorySynopsis: One unfamiliar tree later, Frog and Toad are officially lost, and each is lost in his own way: Toad catastrophizing toward a missed lunch, Frog staying calm with visible effort. Then comes the reframe, explorers do not get lost, they discover, and the woods deliver blueberries, a brook, a grassy nap, and spinning maple seeds. Home finds them by dark, as home does, with Toad refusing a repeat tomorrow and keeping the lovely day anyway, because with a friend you are never truly lost.

stories.situation: Frog is in bed looking quite green, even for a frog, and asks for a made-up story, and Toad has nothing. The hunt goes everywhere: porch pacing, flowerpot searching, pump-splashing, story-shouting, head-standing to shake stories loose, and a full hop-jump-skip-flip routine down the big hill.
stories.coping: Toad returns exhausted and green to find Frog recovered, who retires the request, thanks him for giving it such a good try, and then tells Toad one: the story of a toad who could not think of a story, performed exactly as it just happened, ending with the toad tucked into bed. Failure becomes the story, and being cared for gets returned in kind.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: shake-the-stories-loose comedy plays 2-4; the caring-until-you-drop arc and the story-of-the-day-itself land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'tries everything' is the shape; the script adds each specific failed method, the role reversal, and the story-within-the-story ending.
stories.synopsis: Toad tries everything to think of a story to tell his sick friend.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog is sick and wants only one thing, a story made up out of Toad's imagination, which turns out to be the one thing in the world Toad cannot find. He walks, searches, pumps, shouts, stands on his head, and tumbles down a hill, and comes home empty, dizzy, and green even for a toad. Frog, feeling better, hands the favor back: a story about a toad who could not think of a story, told gently to the friend asleep in his bed.

stories.situation: Toad's mind is filled with everything he has to do, so on Dragonfly's advice he makes a list, and the list becomes the boss: swimming is not on the list, blueberries are not on the list, and letting Frog cross something off is certainly not on the list. Then the wind takes the paper, and running after it is not on the list either.
stories.coping: Frog runs for the list because he has no list, and when it is gone forever, Toad finds the graceful answer: he cannot remember what else was on it, so the only thing to do is sit and do nothing. The day ends with the last item crossed out, go to sleep, and one list amendment from Frog: say good night.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: list-boss comedy plays 2-4; the rigidity-versus-friendship arc, the lost-list crisis, and the doing-nothing resolution land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'blows away in the wind' is the turn; the script adds the list-gags, the not-on-my-list refusals, and the sit-and-do-nothing ending.
stories.synopsis: Toad writes a list of things to do, which blows away in the wind.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Overwhelmed by a busy day, Toad writes a list and discovers the strange comfort of crossing things off, wake up, make breakfast, go to Frog's house. The list starts ruling the day, blocking swims, blueberries, and even a kind Frog holding a pen. When the wind steals it, the crisis dissolves into the best idea yet: with the list gone, there is nothing to do but sit together and do nothing, then cross off go to sleep and add say good night.

stories.situation: Mink's brand-new shoes make Toad want to run fast, jump high, and have lots of fun too, so he buys the last pair at Squirrel's shop and forces them on a size too small. He spends the whole walk insisting they are perfectly fine while they squeak, trip him, and finally land Frog in the mud.
stories.coping: The honest moment arrives on a mud bank: I thought I wanted new shoes, but now I just feel silly, and my feet hurt. Frog's gentle logic reframes them, they were new when you left the store, now they are old shoes, and old shoes he does not need. Toad frees his toes, gives the shoes and their laces to Robin, and rediscovers that his own bare feet walk exactly as fast as he wants.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: too-small-shoe comedy plays 2-4; the wanting-what-someone-else-has arc and the I-feel-silly admission land 5-7. vocabulary gap: Toad's opening pull is envy, not on the 18-term list, so tagged embarrassed/disappointed as nearest. script_vs_synopsis: 'just to be like everyone else' is the motive; the script adds the size-too-small squeeze, the mud fall, and the old-shoes-now reasoning.
stories.synopsis: Toad buys a pair of new shoes just to be like everyone else.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Mink has new shoes, everyone wants to see them, and suddenly Toad does too, never mind that toads do not wear shoes. The purchase fits like a mistake, squeaks like one, and costs him a whole morning of pretending. The release is two-part, admitting the shoes were for looking like Mink rather than for walking like Toad, and gifting them onward, before the best discovery of the day: his own bare feet can wiggle, run, and jump just fine.

stories.situation: A quiet night in is interrupted by the discovery that Toad's special-occasion jacket has sat alone in the dark of the closet for a very long time. The remedy is a manufactured occasion, a night on the town, for the jacket, that escalates through puddle splashes, a rowboat, a swim, every soup on the menu, and a dance that ends in a rip.
stories.coping: The jacket gets its night, and the wearers get theirs, exhausted. The closing arithmetic is the lesson: it was a special occasion, next time the jacket stays home, and the found slippers turn an ordinary night in into exactly the occasion they wanted. Special things, the story suggests, are allowed out on ordinary nights.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: soup-party and dance comedy plays 2-4; the saving-things-for-someday idea and the quiet-night-in payoff land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the jacket premise is new from the script (no catalog synopsis beyond the title pair); the escalation chain and slippers ending are script evidence.
stories.synopsis: Frog helps Toad give his special jacket a night on the town.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog goes hunting for slippers and finds instead a fancy jacket that has been waiting years in the dark for a special occasion that never comes. The cure is immediate: manufacture one. The town tour for the jacket covers puddles, boat trips, a swim, a table for the finest in acorn through plain soup, and one rip too many on the dance floor. The pair tuck the worn-out jacket and themselves back home, where the slippers turn up at last and a quiet night in is revealed as a special occasion of its own.

stories.situation: Toad asks not to be woken, then wakes at afternoon to a full accounting: a picnic breakfast of his favorite things, eaten alone, a two-seat bicycle ridden solo, river-cooling, duck clouds, free ice cream, scarf knitting, and a stage with a band, every moment ending in I wish I had been awake.
stories.coping: Frog closes the tale with the door left open: now that you are awake we can do all those fun things together, and Toad signs up for tomorrow, asking to please be woken. Missing out gets converted into a next time, and the sleepy toad goes back to bed having learned exactly what sleeping in costs.
stories.notes: vibe provisional (drafted from felt energy/tempo; brand-vs-felt rule undecided). mixed age: the picnic-and-bicycle retelling plays 2-4; the missed-out ache, the replayed wish list, and the wake-me-tomorrow turn land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: the retelling structure, the eaten-picnic and stage-dancing beats, and the wake-me-up ending are script evidence (this story's catalog synopsis was not in the quoted set).
stories.synopsis: Frog tells Toad about the adventures Toad missed while he was sleeping in.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Toad bans morning wake-ups and sleeps clean through a day Frog spends wishing he were there. Each I wish I had been awake lands a little heavier until Frog flips it, everything on that list is still available, together. Toad files the lesson where it counts and requests a wake-up call for tomorrow.

stories.situation: Frog's garden produces a squash so big that Toad declares a festival in Frog's honor, and the preparations snowball: hayrides, corn in the hole, a shiny festival hat, and an outfit befitting the grower. stories.synopsis: Toad throws a party in Frog's honor to celebrate a giant squash.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Frog grows a monumental squash and Toad grows the party to match, complete with hayrides, cider, and a spiffy outfit for the frog of the hour. Frog's answer turns the wreckage into the menu, and the festival closes on a table full of squashed squash, a casserole for a best friend, and all's well that ends in a delicious meal.

stories.situation: Winter strips Square of kites, beaches, and apple picking, and he goes quiet and gray with it. stories.situation: Triangle announces Triangle Day, a holiday nobody has heard of, and drags Square and Circle through gift giving, a sacred dance, a triangle song, and repeated marches up the mountain. stories.situation: A big storm rolls in and Triangle wants a front row seat, in a tree, for the spectacle. Circle and Square pull him into the safety cave with hot chocolate, and Triangle keeps hopping back toward the door, certain the amazing thing is outside and the indoors is boring.
stories.coping: The trick is not a lecture, it is a galactic board game and a warm cup: Triangle gets absorbed turn by turn and forgets the show he was missing. He still declares he is going back out, but one more cup and one more game keep him exactly where it is safe.

stories.episodeTitle: Message in a Bottle / Square's Special Place
stories.situation: On beach tidying day Square finds notes in bottles that know his pancake secrets, and he and Triangle spiral into a spy panic, wire their house against imaginary bugs, and dig a trap hole. The spy is Circle, who writes her private thoughts into bottles and drops them in the ocean to let them drift away, and her two friends have now read them twice.
stories.coping: Circle explains what the bottles really were, a way to sort foggy feelings and watch them drift off, and Square and Triangle own the reading outright with a pinkie promise. When they break it anyway and get caught, the apology is harder and more honest: we are terrible friends, we cannot believe us either.
stories.notes: mixed age: the spy-trap slapstick plays 2-4; reading someone's private writing, the pinkie promise broken twice, and earning trust back, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'mysterious bottles on the beach' hides the full spy conspiracy arc and that Circle's coping ritual, not any secret, is what the bottles hold. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Triangle and Square find mysterious bottles on the beach. While playing hide-and-seek, Square discovers a peaceful spot that is just his.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Notes washed up by the storm know things only a spy could know: the cinnamon in Square's pancakes, Triangle's sleep talk, a borrowed yo-yo. The two build a counter-surveillance operation with disguises and a trap hole, and catch exactly one person: Circle, whose private ritual is writing her thoughts into bottles and giving them to the ocean. Twice her friends pry into what she meant to let drift away, and twice the apology has to grow, from pinkie promise to the plain confession that there is no believing them left to do.

stories.situation: Mid-game, Square finds a hollow that fits him exactly, a quiet place of soft bark and embroidered corners that is all his own. Then Triangle and Square's friends wander in, admire the decor, evict the ants, and decide it could be their place, and Square stops coming back.
stories.coping: Square never makes a speech about it; the story lets him keep the place the only way it can be kept after it changes, in memory and in returning to it inside himself whenever the day gets loud. The friends' love is real and still costs him something.
stories.notes: situation note: no starter vocabulary fits, written as needing a special place of one's own, propose addition for vocabulary review. mixed age: hide-and-seek plays 2-4; the bittersweet lesson that sharing a private place changes it, and that you carry it with you, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'discovers a peaceful spot' omits the friends taking it over and the long quiet afterward. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: Triangle and Square find mysterious bottles on the beach. While playing hide-and-seek, Square discovers a peaceful spot that is just his.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Square is losing at shroud-and-find when he drops into a hollow that feels made for him, and something in him goes quiet and glad. After that Square does not return any time soon or any time later, and the story closes on what the hollow taught him: you can always go back to your special place, even if you are not there.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle Goes Solo / Circle Makes a Mistake
stories.situation: Triangle heads into the wild alone to find his true self, unshackled from the crowd of two, with a feather in his cap and no audience. The adventure delivers snakes and deserts, but every triumph goes unapplauded, and he starts narrating to a rock named Rocko.
stories.coping: Triangle never admits the ache directly; he replaces it, naming a rock so there is someone to tell. When Square and Circle confess they followed him out of worry, he gets his audience back and lights up, and only checks that nobody saw the rock conversations.
stories.notes: mixed age: Rocko and the snake stories play 2-4; the question of who an accomplishment is for, when no one is watching, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'sets out on his own' omits the invented audience, the lost-supplies collapse, and that the friends secretly shadowed the whole trip. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The fearless Triangle sets out on his own. Circle leads a journey to ancient ruins and unexpectedly runs into trouble.
stories.perStorySynopsis: Triangle declares independence from the expectations of the crowd, meaning Square and Circle, and sets off to wrestle beasts and discover himself. Alone under an indifferent sky, his feats pile up with no one to tell, so he adopts a rock called Rocko and feeds him ghost stories and achievements alike. It takes losing his supplies to say what the trip was really missing, and just then the truth arrives: his friends followed him the whole way, worried, and Triangle the Great Adventurer gets his audience after all.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle Goes Solo / Circle Makes a Mistake
stories.situation: Circle, the shape who is never wrong, leads her friends to the ancient ruins and forgets two things they cannot do: hover, and outrun a tide. Stranded overnight with no chamomile, no turtle to tuck in, and a boat plan that collapses, she blames Square, then Triangle, then the berries, before the truth lands on her.
stories.coping: Circle says the plain sentence nobody expected from her: it is my fault, I was thinking about myself, and I owe you an apology. Square and Triangle answer with trust instead of a grudge and stories of their own disasters instead of a score.
stories.notes: mixed age: the stranding comedy plays 2-4; the always-right friend making a real mistake and being forgiven, and forgiving herself, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'unexpectedly runs into trouble' hides the blame chain, the crust-eating, and that Circle's apology is the first fault she has ever claimed. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The fearless Triangle sets out on his own. Circle leads a journey to ancient ruins and unexpectedly runs into trouble.

For the first time she owns a mistake out loud, apologizes, and learns that the friends who always mess up are also the friends who always trust, and never keep the ledger.

stories.situation: Square has planned every second of the best sleepover ever, puzzle by timed puzzle, and his guests keep wanting other things: one ghost story, then another, then a pillow fort. stories.coping: Square names what is really hurting, that his idea of fun and his friends' idea have split, and they hear him. The schedule dissolves into an unscheduled pillow fight, and the sleepover that broke the plan turns out better than the plan.

stories.situation: Circle teaches Square to garden, and his first-ever plot comes up greener and juicier than her own. Everyone keeps agreeing his garden is wonderful, and the teacher who has done this for years quietly decides there is no point trying anymore.

A friend who cannot catch anything after two years, and keeps juggling because it is fun, hands her the wisdom without knowing it, and the patch that failed this year still grows a very good salad.

stories.episodeTitle: Triangle and Square's Big Game / The Shooting Star
stories.situation: Circle watches their jumping game once and calls it silly, and the word unhinges its inventors. If the game is silly, maybe they are, and the two retire from games entirely to sit seriously and look at stuff, until they catch Circle alone, playing her own game of rolling in circles until the world goes weird.
stories.coping: Seeing that even Circle has a game nobody else plays unlocks the thought they needed: it is not for us, and it does not have to be. They stop needing her verdict, pick their own game back up, and race each other to the pine tree.
stories.notes: mixed age: the game slapstick plays 2-4; one person's silly making you question the thing you love, and putting it down again, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'feel insecure' is the spine; the script adds the serious-stuff protest, the dizzy-game discovery, and the it's-not-for-us loop that resolves it. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: When Circle brushes off their game, Triangle and Square feel insecure. A mysterious meteor crash inspires a treasure hunt.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The Leapstravaganza has everything, jumping, leaping, goggles, and one spectator verdict: silly. Triangle and Square take the word home and dissect it until the game they made up feels unsalvageable, then retire to the serious sport of looking at stuff. Catching Circle mid-roll in her own private dizzy game teaches them the thing no pep talk could, that games do not have to be for everyone to be worth playing, and the rematch to the pine tree is on.

stories.episodeTitle: Narrator's Big Day / Square's Time Chest
stories.situation: Nothing is happening on The Island, and the Narrator's job is to observe and tell, never to change or affect the story. She confesses how hard that is, how she wishes she could make her own stories instead of waiting for one to show up, right before a beetle egg hatches into the little grub she names Sarah.
stories.coping: Watching Sarah crawl, nearly freeze, and nearly become a bird's lunch pushes the Narrator past the rule that narrators stay out of it: she speaks up, tells the bird to drop that bug, and it does. She saves the story herself and finds a voice she did not know she had.
stories.notes: mixed age: the egg-to-beetle bug saga plays 2-4; the meta idea of a narrator who is only supposed to watch, and the choice to break a rule to help, land 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'gives Narrator time to herself' hides that the whole story is the beetle's one-day metamorphosis and that the Narrator intervenes. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The Shapes' rather ordinary day gives Narrator time to herself. Square struggles to find the perfect object for the island's new time capsule.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The Island has nothing going on, and the Narrator, whose whole job is to wait for stories, admits how lonely that can feel. Then a leaf hides a Drabling Beetle egg, and she pours herself into the little grub she names Sarah: first meal, harrowing pinecone, cocoon surprise, and one very hungry bird. A narrator is not supposed to change the story, but she talks the bird into dropping Sarah anyway, and the voice she found stays with her long after the beetle flies off.

stories.coping: Under gentle pressure from two detectives who genuinely want to help, Square admits the thing he called silly: the toast he never got to give, and the times his friends walked away mid-moment. They apologize, and when Turtle the bloodhound locates the mug, the postponed toast finally happens.
stories.notes: mixed age: the mugnapping investigation plays 2-4; the buried hurt underneath a small crisis, and finding the courage to say the silly feeling out loud, lands 5-7. script_vs_synopsis: 'island-wide hunt' skips that the clue trail is really Square's own unspoken feelings, and that the mug was in the picnic basket all along. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The disappearance of Square's favorite mug sends him on an island-wide hunt. Triangle bets Circle that he can stay perfectly still for ten minutes.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The morning starts with a missing mug and ends with a solved friendship. stories.notes: mixed age: ants and the itch acknowledgment play 2-4; the felt difference between sitting still and actually being present, lands 5-7 too. script_vs_synopsis: 'bets Circle that he can stay perfectly still' is right; the script adds the internal visit from his own itch and the last-second forfeit that shows he meditated for the feeling, not the prize. confidence high.
stories.synopsis: The disappearance of Square's favorite mug sends him on an island-wide hunt. Triangle bets Circle that he can stay perfectly still for ten minutes.

stories.coping: He follows the strange creatures instead of unpacking, hides what he is to stay, and when a storm cloud creature melts down he names his own inside spaghetti and fireworks and offers it a hug. The hug works, the professor lets him stay, and the mask stays on by choice.

stories.situation: Loroc declares himself savior of the planet and blocks the way, Eight confronts Eva as one of them, and Rovender falls in the fighting. stories.synopsis: With the fate of the planet at stake, Eva races to deliver the Heart to the thermal vent, and Eight must choose between the war she built and the family that never left her.
stories.perStorySynopsis: The finale keeps every promise the series made: Loroc's savior act collapses, Vanpa's magnet trap and the Fours sign-off buy the tunnel, and the creatures Eva once saved come back for her when the way is sealed. Rovender falls, asking only that she not let this change her, and it is Eight, finally given the jargum to hear Orbona speak, who breaks: the Heart greets her the way it once greeted Eva, with there is no them, only us, and the sister who ordered the war chooses re-entry, home, and love.
